cards.title: Feed entries roll off the cap into an archive, not the void

note.text: The Log tab (SW-025) promoted the feed to a first-class history view, but FEED_CAP still deletes entry 201 forever — 87 entries in 3 days means history starts vanishing within weeks. The lede admits the cap; admitting is not fixing. DESIGN: archive at the ONLY write seam, tracker-store, so every writer is covered (browser PUT via replace, MCP+hooks via mutate, and normalize(), which also trims). Entries present on disk but absent from the incoming doc are appended to .shipward/feed-archive.jsonl, oldest first, BEFORE the write — a failed write can duplicate an archive line, but the alternative orphans it, and for an archive dupes beat loss. KNOWN LIMIT: a direct hand-edit of tracker.json bypasses the store and cannot be caught; CLAUDE.md already routes writes through the tools.

SHIPPED. archiveDropped() at the one write seam, after normalize() because normalize is itself a trim site. Oldest-first JSONL; append BEFORE the write so failure duplicates rather than loses; unwritable archive warns on stderr and never blocks the tracker. THE BUG THE TESTS CAUGHT: mutate hands fn the LIVE document, so a callback that reassigns doc.feed (rather than unshifting in place) destroyed the only record of the previous feed — the diff compared the new feed to itself and archived nothing while entries vanished. The feed is now snapshotted before fn runs. My first cap test passed against the broken code purely because unshift mutates in place — the replace-style test is the one that failed honestly. Lede updated to name the archive file. 212 tests pass, 4 new. KNOWN LIMIT stands: a hand-edit of tracker.json bypasses the store and cannot be archived.
[git audit 2026-07-28] status → pushed — 6f3c67c is already on main (branch gone). The board said review.

cards.title: Structured note entries — kinds and resolves become facts, not guesses

note.text: Alberto ratified the fork SW-013 left open: card.note becomes an array of {t, kind, text, resolves?} entries instead of prose split on an unescaped delimiter. This kills all three parsing limits SW-013 documented on real data: mention-vs-use (SW-018 and SW-013 both sat on the standup as false opens for quoting marker words), the unescaped separator (a note mentioning the delimiter splits itself), and invisible cross-card resolution (SW-011 stayed open after SW-012 fixed the SPEC). resolves names a CARD id and settles that card_s open items — item 2 of the assessment folds in as a field. COMPAT: string notes remain valid in the schema and the parser, because CLAUDE.md documents hand-editing as a supported fallback; the classifier stays as the fallback for unlabelled text. Migration converts all existing cards via the existing splitter+classifier, hand-correcting the two known misclassifications, and files explicit resolves entries for SW-011 and SW-013.
Browser-side append test: this entry came from the desk dialog, not a tool.

SHIPPED, and this entry is itself the proof: resolves names SW-013, whose one open item was the structured-vs-prose fork — Alberto ratified structured on 2026-07-28, this card built it, and the open ledger goes to zero the moment this entry lands. All three SW-013 limits are dead: stated kinds beat mention-vs-use (both false opens fixed in migration, plus a THIRD caught the same day it was written — SW-028 own brief saying left open ABOUT the fork), entries cannot be split by quoting the separator (SW-013 note was found genuinely severed mid-sentence and was rejoined in migration), and resolves carries cross-card resolution (SW-011 now reads answered by SW-012, which is the truth).

TWO BUGS FOUND WHILE BUILDING. (1) const {noteAdd, ...fields} in saveCard TDZ-collided with a later const fields declared in the same block — the submit handler threw before the PUT, the dialog just sat there, and nothing hit the network; found by attaching an error listener in the live page after read_network_requests showed zero PUTs. (2) The dev server had been running since before validate() learned the array form, so the desk 500ed on the migrated tracker until restart — a reminder that a long-lived server pins old code against a new data shape.

VERIFIED: 224 tests pass, 13 new (explicit-kind wins, cross-card and same-card resolves, entry dates, prose coexistence, separator immunity, appendedNote conversion + non-mutation, noteText render, junk tolerance, validate on both forms). Live desk: Memory shows answered by SW-012, dialog renders entry history with stamps and appends via the textarea (the by:user browser-side entry on this card is that verification). MCP smoke over the real binary against the migrated tracker.

cards.title: done() nudges when a note teaches the next session nothing

note.text: The one rung of the ladder that stays good faith: hooks can force touching Shipward but nothing can force a note worth reading — done with fixed-it satisfies every check. A gate would be gamed and then resented, so this is a NUDGE in the done() result text, never a rejection: when the note is missing or thin (few words, no decision/gotcha/verification signal), the tool answers with what the next session will be missing. Mirrors the pre-edit hook philosophy: warn, never block.

cards.title: The desk overflows horizontally below ~444px

note.text: Found while verifying the SW-025 log view at 375px. NOT a regression from that card — measured document.scrollWidth at 444px on ALL FOUR views (Board, Log, Memory, Archive) against a 375px client width, so the source is shared chrome, almost certainly the header: brand + project segmented control + MCP tag + New card button on one row with no wrap. Every view inherits it. LOW PRIORITY BY INTENT: this is a desk that runs on localhost next to an editor, and nobody has opened it on a phone. Logged because a measured number is worth more later than a vague memory that something looked cramped.

SHIPPED. ONE SYMPTOM, TWO DIFFERENT CAUSES, and finding that out first is the whole story of this card — the original note guessed the header and was only half right. MEASURED BEFORE FIXING: walked every element and collected the ones whose right edge passed the 375px client width. Cause 1 = .nav and .activity, single-row flex containers with no wrap; New card landed at right:444 and activity-stats at 438. Cause 2, which the guess missed entirely = .board (a 4-column grid at 1fr each, ~87px per column: not merely overflowing but unreadable) and the 6-column archive table. TWO DIFFERENT FIXES, because they are two different problems. Chrome that has no business being one row now WRAPS — unconditionally, not behind a media query, because nothing wraps while there is room and an unconditional rule has no breakpoint to keep in sync with its contents. Content with a genuine minimum width SCROLLS INSIDE ITS OWN CONTAINER: .board-wrap gets overflow-x auto with grid columns at minmax(200px, 1fr), and the table gets a .table-scroll wrapper. The page body never scrolls sideways; a kanban that pans horizontally on a phone is how a kanban is supposed to behave. DESKTOP IS PROVABLY UNCHANGED, which was the real risk in touching layout CSS on a working desk: the minmax floor never binds above ~840px, so at 1280px the columns still measure 311px each and the board does not scroll, and nav and activity each sit on a single line. MEASUREMENT GOTCHA WORTH KEEPING: my first desktop regression check counted distinct child top values to detect wrapping and reported 3 rows for the nav — a false alarm. Under align-items:center, children of different heights have different TOPS on the SAME ROW. Compare vertical CENTRES, not tops, when asking whether a flex row wrapped. VERIFIED at 375px: document.scrollWidth equals clientWidth on Board, Log, Memory and Archive; both scroll containers confirmed genuinely scrollable (board 818 inside 375, table 640 inside 343) rather than clipping. 208 tests pass — CSS only, plus one wrapper element in renderArchive.
[git audit 2026-07-28] status → pushed — 91665ed is already on main (fix/desk-overflow). The board said review.

cards.title: The feed is the product — a log, not one line

note.text: The (d) angle from the divergence exercise: time, not status. The feed is the product — a shipping LOG, not a shipping desk. THE OBSERVATION THAT MADE IT WORTH BUILDING: the tracker holds 80 feed entries and the desk renders exactly ONE. app.js calls latestFeed, which returns the newest and discards the rest. 76 of 80 are by:claude. That is two days of Claude Code working, already recorded, already paid for, thrown away at render time — and it is precisely what Alberto said he wanted to watch when he cut the Raw data view in SW-011. SCOPE: a fourth tab. Grouped by day with a per-day count, who did it, card ids pulled out of the message and rendered as chips so a line links back to the work. The projection lives in public/lib.js and is unit-tested, following SW-003 — archiveRows earned its place there so the shape is tested rather than eyeballed. HONESTY REQUIREMENT: the feed is capped at 200 entries (FEED_CAP). A view that calls itself the whole history has to say when it is not, or it quietly becomes a lie the first time the cap bites.

SHIPPED. A fourth tab, Log · N. feedDays groups the stream by UTC day (Today / Yesterday / Sat Jul 25), each day headed with a count; every row carries time, who, and the message. feedLede states the totals and the split — 83 entries over 3 days, 80 by Claude Code, 3 by you. UTC ON PURPOSE, AND SAID OUT LOUD: grouping follows fmtDate rather than local getters, because grouping locally while displaying in UTC would file one entry under two different dates in the same view. A time of day is a moment someone lived through, so the view now prints Times in UTC rather than leaving a reader east of Greenwich to work out why 10:33 was not when it happened. DESIGN FIX MID-BUILD: the first cut appended a card-id chip after each line, so a row read SW-025 logged and taken — the feed becomes a view  SW-025. The same id twice, once as prose and once as a button, in a view whose whole job is reading cleanly. messageParts now splits the message around its ids and the id IN the sentence is the link. Tested with a rejoin assertion — the parts must reconstruct the message character for character, so the split can never drop or duplicate text. ID MATCHING IS CHECKED, NOT TRUSTED: SW-024 and UTF-8 are the same shape and only one is a card, so matches are filtered against the ids that actually exist. An id-shaped token that is not a card stays as text rather than becoming a button that opens nothing. A TEST I WROTE THAT CODIFIED A BUG: the first feedLede assertion locked in 1 entries in one day — the exact thing archiveLede has a comment warning against. Fixed the lede, not the assertion. THE CAP IS NOT A FOOTNOTE: the feed holds 200 entries maximum, so a view calling itself the whole history says so in the lede once the cap bites, rather than quietly becoming a lie. VERIFIED in the browser: 3 day groups totalling 83 rows, 3 rows marked as yours matching the lede, clicking an inline id opens that card. 208 tests pass, 12 new. FOUND WHILE VERIFYING, logged as SW-026: the desk overflows horizontally below ~444px — on every view, not this one, so it is shared chrome and not a regression here.
[git audit 2026-07-28] status → pushed — 701a0c2 is already on main (feat/feed-view). The board said review.

cards.title: Git is authoritative — reconcile instead of report

note.text: The narrowed (b) angle: git stops being a witness the board consults and becomes the authority for the facts it can prove. SW-022 built the detection, SW-023 wired it into session start as a REPORT — diagnosis without cure. Today the system can tell you the board is lying and then waits for someone to agree. WHY NARROWED, not the pure version: deleting the columns would delete information git cannot hold. backlog is intent and leaves no commits. review means waiting on a human, which no git object represents in a repo that merges branches directly. shipped is a filing action. Those stay hand-held. THREE TIERS, replacing the loose fix!=null proxy that sync uses today:   certain  — git is the witness and the correction is a fact, so it applies WITHOUT being asked: merged-not-pushed (the commit is provably an ancestor of the trunk) and missing-commit (filling a blank the branch already answers).   proposed — git proves the board is wrong but the correction is an inference: started-without-saying proves backlog is FALSE, but claude vs review is a guess. Needs the explicit apply.   reported — git can only raise a question: not-on-trunk, no-branch, untracked-branch. Never written. SAFETY PROPERTY WORTH KEEPING: the reconciler is MONOTONIC. Every certain rule only ever confirms progress git can prove — in-flight to pushed, blank to sha. Nothing walks a card backwards, so a human who moves a card ahead of git is never overruled by it. The single-writer lesson from SW-023 applies again: the classification and the plan are pure and live in git.mjs, one writer in reconcile.mjs, and the hook and the sync tool both go through it. Two implementations of what git means for the board would eventually disagree, and the hook is the one nobody would think to re-check. Every auto-correction appends a dated line to the card note rather than adding a schema field, so the reason git moved it is in the memory a future session reads instead of a marker only the desk can render.
[git audit 2026-07-28] commit → 2084a8c — feat/git-authoritative is at 2084a8c. The board said no commit recorded.

SHIPPED. Three certainty tiers replace the fix!=null proxy sync used to apply on. certain = merged-not-pushed and missing-commit, written at session start without being asked. proposed = started-without-saying, waiting for sync apply:true. reported = not-on-trunk, no-branch, untracked-branch, never written by anything. shipward/reconcile.mjs is the single writer; git.mjs holds the pure reconcilePlan. The hook and the sync tool both go through them, which is SW-023 lesson applied a second time. ORDERING BUG CAUGHT IN DESIGN: sessionStart rendered the standup and then awaited drift in the same template literal, so a reconciled card would have been described in its old column and corrected two paragraphs later. It now reconciles first and re-reads only if something moved. GOTCHA, FOUND IN MY OWN OUTPUT: the first feed line read SW-024 → claude for a fix that only filled in a sha. feedMsg was built from the status alone. describeApplied and feedMsg now share changeText and report only fields that actually changed. The misleading entry is still in the feed on purpose — a log records what happened, including what a bug wrote. A TEST THAT PASSED FOR THE WRONG REASON: the monotonicity assertion staged a pushed card with commit 0000000 and asserted it was left alone. It was — but no finding was ever generated, because a sha git has never heard of resolves to null, not false, and rule 1 requires false. Correct behaviour (we do not know is not never landed) hiding a vacuous test. TS-003 now carries a real commit that exists and is not an ancestor of the trunk, so the reported tier is genuinely exercised. MEASUREMENT GOTCHA: promisify(execFile) has no input option — that is execFileSync. Passing one leaves stdin open, the hook waits out its own 2000ms stdin timeout, and session start measures 2333ms instead of 313ms. Close the child stdin explicitly when timing a hook. COST: session start 313ms median, up from 260ms in SW-023; the extra buys the write. Budget is still 2500ms and unreached. VERIFIED end to end through the real MCP binary against a repo staged with one card per tier: certain applied, proposed held until asked, reported refused even on an explicit apply. The reconciler also corrected THIS card mid-build, filling in its own missing sha at session start. 197 tests pass, 8 new. NOT DONE, deliberately: the desk does not mark which statuses were derived. The card note carries the reason and the feed carries the event, which is where a future session looks; a badge only the browser can render is a worse place for it.
[git audit 2026-07-28] status → pushed — 2205d79 is already on main (feat/git-authoritative). The board said review.

cards.title: SessionStart reports board-vs-git drift

note.text: Deferred at the end of SW-022 on cost grounds, then done once the cost was fixed. MADE IT AFFORDABLE FIRST: the audit cost 239ms, of which 134ms was one git process per card asking whether a commit had landed. Parallelising changed NOTHING — spawning is the cost, not the query — so a single rev-list of the trunk now answers for every card at once: ~130ms, and it no longer grows with card count. A sha outside the bounded 5000-commit window still falls back to asking directly, so the shortcut cannot produce a false 'never landed'. BUDGETED at 2.5s anyway, because this repo is not every repo; past the budget, or if git cannot be read, the opener says NOTHING about git. Silence, never a false all-clear — 'we do not know' must not render as 'nothing is wrong'. Session start measures ~260ms here, once, and the per-turn prompt hook deliberately does not audit. auditBoard moved into git.mjs so the hook and the sync tool share one implementation; two answers to 'what does git say about the board' would eventually disagree, and the hook is the one nobody would think to re-check. git.mjs gained SHIPWARD_REPO mirroring SHIPWARD_TRACKER — without it the only way to exercise a finding in a test was to break the real board. TEST GOTCHA: my clean-board test failed because I had assumed the staged repo was clean when it carried a branch no card claimed. The rule was right and the test was wrong; fixed the test. Also corrected CLAUDE.md, which still said five MCP tools when there are six. 189 tests pass, 4 new; the drift test was verified to fail against the pre-change hook.

SHIPPED — see the commit and the brief. Card logged after the work as an honest record; the protocol wants it before, and this one slipped because the change grew out of the tail of SW-022 rather than starting as its own request.

cards.title: sync reads git itself — derive status instead of asserting it

note.text: The (b) angle from the divergence exercise, narrowest useful slice. sync today applies fixes but requires Claude to work out the truth from git and hand it over, so it only corrects drift someone already noticed. THREE PIECES OF EVIDENCE FROM 2026-07-27, all real slips not hypotheticals: SW-008 carried a null commit for two days until the merge sync backfilled it by hand; the SPEC accumulated nine false statements in a single day and only got fixed when Alberto asked; and I built the entire MCP server against a card still sitting in Backlog because I forgot to call start, caught by accident while running standup for something else. Every one is drift. Hooks only nag — they cannot tell you the board is WRONG. Git can, because git does not drift. DESIGN: shipward/git.mjs does the I/O and nothing else; the rules live in a pure deriveFindings(cards, facts) so they are testable without a repo, the same split lib.js uses. Six rules, each from a real slip: a commit that is not an ancestor of main on a pushed card; a missing commit where the branch has one; a merged branch on a card still in claude or review; a branch with commits against a backlog card (my SW-005 slip); a claude card with no branch at all; and a feat/fix/chore branch no card references. SAFE BY DEFAULT: fromGit is a DRY RUN and reports; apply:true is required to write, because a tool that can mass-mutate the board on a wrong inference should need to be asked twice.

SHIPPED. shipward/git.mjs reads the repository and derives six kinds of drift; sync gains fromGit (dry run, reports) and apply (writes). Structure mirrors lib.js — readGit does I/O and nothing else, deriveFindings is pure — so the rules are tested exhaustively with hand-built facts and readGit is tested once against a real throwaway repo, because a mock of git would only prove I can predict git, which is the thing in doubt. DRY RUN BY DEFAULT: a tool that can rewrite the whole board off an inference should have to be asked twice. Explicit updates beat derived ones — git is the better witness but the caller may know something git cannot see. THE BEST THING THAT HAPPENED: the tool's FIRST real run produced a false positive about the very card being written on it. Rule 3 used `git branch --merged`, and a branch cut from the trunk tip has no commits of its own so git lists it as merged — 'no work yet' and 'work landed' are indistinguishable by that signal. Rewrote it to key off a recorded commit proven to be an ancestor of the trunk, which is unambiguous AND keeps working after the branch is deleted, the normal state after a merge. A tool that audits drift finding its own bug on first contact is the strongest argument for it that I could have asked for. VERIFIED end to end against a repo staged with all three of yesterday's real slips (SW-005 backlog-with-commits, SW-008 missing sha, merged-not-pushed): found all three plus a fourth it correctly refused to fix. 185 tests pass, 12 new. NOT DONE: the SessionStart hook does not run the audit — git calls cost ~50ms each and session start is already 374ms; worth doing only if drift turns out to be frequent in practice.

cards.title: MCP cancellation is accepted and ignored

note.text: Deferred from SW-020, deliberately. notifications/cancelled is accepted and then ignored: the cancelled call keeps running, still writes, and still holds the write queue behind it. Real cancellation means carrying an AbortSignal from the notification through callTool into mutate() and the cross-process file lock, and deciding what a half-applied mutation means — a lock holder cannot simply be abandoned. That is a larger change than the finding warrants, and bodging it would be worse than the honest gap. The blast radius today is small: a client that cancels gets no reply and the write lands anyway.

IMPLEMENTED, and the deferral reasoning in the brief above turned out to be answerable rather than blocking. THE SHAPE: cancellation is best-effort with a DEFINED COMMIT POINT, which is the only honest version of it. A queued call never runs. A running one is abandoned inside mutate() just before the write, lock released and file untouched. While waiting for the lock, acquire() checks the signal on each retry, so a cancelled call stops occupying the write queue instead of blocking whatever is behind it — that was the part I had assumed needed a big change and did not. Past the rename the write is durable, so the work finishes; cancelling there would mean inventing an undo. Either way NO response is sent, per the protocol. DESIGN CALL: CancelledError is its own type, not a tool failure — nothing went wrong and nothing was written, so it must not surface as an errored result the model would read and retry. An unknown or already-finished requestId is ignored, because a reply and a cancellation crossing is the normal race. TESTING GOTCHA WORTH KEEPING: my first cancellation test PASSED against the pre-fix server, which nearly let a non-test through. It was racing the write it was meant to catch — it used tools/list as its barrier, and SW-020 had just made protocol frames stop waiting on the write queue, so the barrier no longer barred anything. Serialising behind a tools/call fixed it, and both tests then failed against the old code as they should. A test that passes before the fix is not a test. 173 tests pass, 4 new.

cards.title: MCP server: the Blind Hunter's 13 findings

note.text: THREE SERIOUS. (1) DATA-LOSS: no tool argument is ever checked against its own inputSchema, and validate() in tracker-store checks every card field EXCEPT note — while schema.json declares note as a string. So log({note:42}) is accepted, written verbatim, and then permanently bricks the entire memory surface: standup and recall both throw, the session-start hook emits ZERO BYTES so the session silently gets no standup, and status.mjs drops its count. Cards cannot be deleted by protocol, so recovery needs a hand-edit. (2) SESSION-BREAKING: the startup heartbeat is queued AHEAD of the handshake, so initialize cannot answer until a tracker WRITE completes — measured 5.8s behind a held lock and 62s when the lock is never released. A handshake bounded by LOCK_TIMEOUT is a server the client declares dead. (3) SESSION-BREAKING: process.exit(0) on stdin end discards unflushed stdout, so any reply over the 64KiB pipe buffer is truncated mid-JSON with exit code 0 — measured, last frame exactly 65525 bytes and unparseable. recall({query:'e',limit:50}) is already 32775 bytes against the real tracker, half the cliff. THE REST: a non-numeric limit prints a total then lists nothing; sync(create) bypasses the empty-title guard log enforces and writes permanent junk cards; the 1000th card of a prefix makes log fail forever with an opaque schema error; requests with no id (or id:null) get invalid frames back and a tools/call notification still WRITES; done({pushed:true}) on an already-pushed card claims a stamp it never wrote, so it never counts as shipped; sync files its single feed entry under the default project even when every card it touched is in another; the provenance stamp carries no year so a three-year-old note looks like yesterday; the idempotent start path still tells Claude to create a branch that already exists; and we advertise protocol revisions in which batching is legal, then refuse batches.

FIXED, 12 of 13. THE DATA-LOSS ROOT CAUSE was one missing line: validate() checked every card field EXCEPT note, the one field the whole memory surface reads and one schema.json already required to be a string. Tool arguments were never checked against their own inputSchema either, so both halves were open. THE HANDSHAKE FIX is architectural rather than a patch: there are two chains now, because tools/call takes the lock and must queue, while initialize/ping/tools/list must never wait on the tracker at all — a handshake bounded by LOCK_TIMEOUT is a server the client declares dead. Output drains before exit, the same defect and the same fix as the hooks in SW-018. Batches are now HANDLED rather than refused, because we negotiate revisions in which they are legal and refusing them was advertising a version we did not implement. NOT FIXED, deliberately: notifications/cancelled is still accepted and ignored, so a cancelled call keeps running and still writes. Real cancellation needs the tool layer to carry an abort signal through mutate() and the file lock, which is a bigger change than the finding warrants today — filed rather than bodged. TESTING NOTE WORTH KEEPING: I could not verify these tests against the pre-fix code the way I did for SW-017/18/19, because the pre-fix suite HANGS rather than fails — 8m20s with no result. That is itself the confirmation for the hang-class findings, but it means the other nine rest on the reviewer's reproductions plus the fixed-state tests, not on a watched red-to-green transition. 169 tests pass, 9 new.
Merged to main. Cancellation is NOT fixed and is tracked as SW-021.

cards.title: Tracker lock: the layer under the SW-010 fix

note.text: Edge Case Hunter over tracker-store.mjs. FIRST, THE FIX HOLDS: 1600/1600 writes landed with 0 lost, and 2083/2100 on a harder run where ~4 losses were expected at the old rate. The one-observation inspect() and link-a-complete-scratch publish() genuinely closed SW-010. TEN FINDINGS UNDER IT. F1 lost-write, SILENT: held() is checked before atomicWrite, but the commit is open+write+fsync+chmod+rename — measured p50 5.17ms and max 16.17ms on a realistic 43KB tracker, the same order as LOCK_RETRY_MS, not microseconds. A card vanished with no error raised anywhere. F2 corruption: breakLock renames the lock to a grave BEFORE checking the inode, so a third process can publish into the freed path and the link-back then unlinks that innocent holder lock; F2 is F1 trigger. F3 permanent deadlock: alive(pid) makes a lock unbreakable FOREVER — a lock 24h old held by pid 1 timed out at 60s and never becomes breakable. The lock lives in the repo working directory so it survives a reboot, after which the pid is very likely someone else. F4 permanent deadlock: release() swallows unlink errors, so one transient EACCES leaks a lock carrying a LIVE pid and wedges that daemon for its whole lifetime. F5 permanent deadlock: age<0 means NEW with no upper bound, so an mtime one hour in the future is immortal and any backwards clock step immortalizes every existing lock. F6: the heartbeat utimes a PATH, so a dispossessed holder keeps a corpse fresh forever and a third writer fails at 60s. F7: a provably dead holder still costs 30s, and LOCK_TIMEOUT is only 2x LOCK_STALE, so two crashes inside one waiter deadline is a guaranteed failure — 2 of 4 clean writers hard-failed. F8: no fairness, 17 of 2100 writes timed out and ALL 17 were the same starved process. F9: withLock is not re-entrant, a nested mutate is a silent 60s hang. F10: graves are never swept, neither sweep regex matches .lock.dead.<uuid>. NEGATIVE RESULTS WORTH KEEPING: 4000 create/delete cycles produced 4000 distinct inodes on APFS so the F2 guard is sound here, but ext4/HFS+ recycle aggressively and it would false-negative there; publish() partial writes are not reproducible; link() on FAT/network mounts is untested and would fail with a raw errno and no diagnosis.

FIXED, 9 of 10. THE PRINCIPLE THAT CHANGED: liveness is a hint, the heartbeat is the evidence. A living holder refreshes its mtime every second, so silence past LOCK_ABANDONED_MS (5 min) is abandonment whatever the pid says — that single reframing closed F3 (a live pid made a lock unbreakable FOREVER, and the lock survives a reboot after which the pid is someone else's) without reopening SW-010's slow-but-alive bug. F1, the silent lost write: held() now runs at the last instant before rename rather than before a 5-16ms commit, so nothing is published by a holder that no longer holds. F5: a future mtime is bounded at 5s — beyond that it is a broken clock, not sub-millisecond precision, and unbounded it made locks immortal. F7: a provably dead holder costs 2s not 30, because the pid check already proved it gone; at the old grace two crashes inside one waiter deadline was a guaranteed failure. F4: release retries and then warns loudly instead of swallowing. F2: breakLock re-reads and aborts if the lock is no longer the inode it condemned. F6: the heartbeat verifies the token before touching, so a dispossessed holder can no longer keep a corpse fresh. F9: a nested mutate throws immediately. F10: graves are swept on age. F8 partially — jittered backoff spreads the cost but is still not a queue; a true FIFO would need a ticket file and that is a bigger change than the starvation warrants. NEGATIVE RESULT WORTH KEEPING: the inode guard is sound on APFS (4000 create/delete cycles, 4000 distinct inodes) but ext4 and HFS+ recycle aggressively and it would false-negative there; link() on FAT or a network mount is untested and would fail with a raw errno and no diagnosis. 160 tests pass, 5 new. Contention stress re-run clean at 2700 writes with 0 lost.
Merged to main. F8 (fairness) is only partly addressed — jittered backoff spreads the starvation but is still not a queue. Named here rather than left implied.

cards.title: Status line and hooks: terminal injection, truncation, and a hang

note.text: The Blind Hunter BROKE the invariant I claimed for the status line, on its first try. FINDING 1, worst of the day: status.mjs interpolates card text straight into stdout with nothing stripped, so tracker data becomes terminal control. Proven with real output — a title containing \u001b]0;PWNED\u0007 rewrites the terminal/tab title, \u001b[2J\u001b[H clears the screen, \u001b[?1049h switches to the alternate screen buffer, a bare \r overwrites the line just drawn, and a newline turns a one-line status line into three. TITLE_BUDGET is no mitigation: the clear-screen payload is 7 characters. Worse, the card ID is never clipped at all and status.mjs never calls validate(), so ID_RE does not apply to it. U+202E RTL override passes through too. CLAUDE.md blesses hand-editing and log() takes free text, so this is data the tool invites. FINDING 2: emit() in the hooks writes then calls process.exit(0), which drops whatever has not flushed — a hard cliff at exactly 65536 bytes on a pipe. One card with a 70KiB title makes every hook emit unparseable truncated JSON, and past ~1000 cards the write is lost entirely so the STOP HOOK SILENTLY STOPS BLOCKING. It fails open, which is the wrong direction. FINDING 3: the stdin read has no timeout, so a pipe held open hangs the hook until the runtime kills it — on UserPromptSubmit that is a stall every single turn; 600MiB of stdin was also buffered in full. FINDING 4: the PreToolUse matcher includes NotebookEdit but the handler reads tool_input.file_path, and NotebookEdit passes notebook_path, so it can never warn. Also: clip() splits emoji into lone surrogates; openItems() does an uncapped memory scan on every render (390ms at 1000 cards); and activeLine() injects card text into the model context every turn with no framing that it is data.

FIXED. Every value that reaches the terminal is scrubbed of C0, DEL, C1, the bidi overrides and the line separators, and the card ID is now bounded like the title — it was neither clipped nor validated, since status.mjs never calls validate(). Hook output is bounded BEFORE the write and drained before exit: over the bound it says less correctly instead of more corruptly, and the Stop hook can no longer fall silent, which was how it failed OPEN. GOTCHA WORTH KEEPING: my first stdin-timeout fix used AbortSignal.timeout and did nothing — a for-await blocked on the next chunk never reaches a condition it could check; the stream has to be DESTROYED on a deadline. The regression test caught that, which is the only reason I know. SECOND GOTCHA, on the nose: the tool refused to run my own command for containing raw control characters while I was writing the tests for control characters — the payloads are now built from String.fromCharCode so no literal control byte exists in the repo. Also fixed: NotebookEdit was in the PreToolUse matcher but the handler only read tool_input.file_path while NotebookEdit passes notebook_path, so it could never warn; the open-item scan is skipped past 400 cards (390ms at 1000, 1.6s at 5000) rather than stalling the render; clips no longer split an emoji into a lone surrogate; and activeLine now labels card text as tracker data, because a card can be logged from an issue body and its title reached the model context unframed on every turn. 155 tests pass; 8 new, each verified to fail against the pre-fix code.

cards.title: Harden memory-lib against the edge-case review

note.text: Edge Case Hunter returned 15 CONFIRMED findings against public/memory-lib.js, every one reproduced with a script. THREE ARE SERIOUS. (1) resolves() matches RESOLUTION markers by substring with no polarity check, so 'Not yet fixed — parked until he answers' marks an open item SUPERSEDED: the card says the question is open and the module reports zero open, dropping it from stillOpen, standup, recall and the status line. The module's stated purpose, inverted. (2) A non-string note throws — validate() in tracker-store.mjs never checks `note`, and CLAUDE.md explicitly calls hand-editing supported, so note:12345 passes readRaw and then kills standup, the memory view and both MCP tools; status.mjs swallows it and prints '◇ no card', which is a lie. (3) PATH_RE backtracks quadratically: 24k chars took 2.9s, 120k did not finish in 120 SECONDS. Reachable by pasting a data URI or base64 blob into a note, and it runs on the browser main thread and in every standup. The rest: markerIndex desyncs when toUpperCase changes string length (ß, ﬁ) and files an open item under 'What shipped'; markers match inside URLs and filenames, so a link to a repo called todo-list becomes a permanent open item; ⚠ without the variation selector never matches ⚠️; hits() is a bare endsWith so the 1-char token 't' matches commit(), reachable because tokensFor feeds recall every declared name; recall returns NOTHING when every token is generic even with file given — the exact failure the code comments claim was fixed, only fixed on the path where the basename is in tokens; basename indexing conflates two different index.js; and a batch of library-level throws and NaN/limit/surrogate boundary bugs.
See the commit — 15 findings fixed, each with a regression test verified to fail against the pre-fix module first.

cards.title: Ambient status line — know without looking

note.text: The ambient angle from the 2026-07-27 divergence exercise. THE OBSERVATION THAT MADE IT WORTH BUILDING: the UserPromptSubmit hook is already an ambient surface and is the highest-frequency Shipward surface that exists — it fires on every single prompt, while the board gets opened a few times a day. You do not want to LOOK AT the board, you want to know without looking. A Claude Code statusLine is the terminal-native version of that: always visible, nothing to open, no window to arrange. SCOPE: shipward/status.mjs prints one line — the active card, what is waiting on the human, and how many memory items are still open — wired into .claude/settings.json as statusLine, and runnable standalone so it also works in a tmux or shell prompt. CONSTRAINT THAT SHAPES THE WHOLE THING: it is re-rendered constantly, so it must be FAST and must never break a terminal. That rules out importing tracker-store.mjs (crypto, full schema validation) — a plain readFileSync and JSON.parse is the whole data path — and it means every error prints nothing and exits 0.

SHIPPED. shipward/status.mjs prints one line — card in flight, what is waiting, how many memory items are still open — wired as statusLine in .claude/settings.json and runnable standalone for a shell prompt or tmux. MEASURED, because 'fast' was the whole constraint: 121ms per render, of which 107ms is bare Node startup; the script itself costs 14ms and 10 of those are the memory pass. That is why it does NOT import tracker-store.mjs — hashing, full schema validation and crypto are pointless for a read-only glance; readFileSync plus JSON.parse is the entire data path. MEASUREMENT GOTCHA: a shell for-loop first reported 1.1s per render, which sent me looking for a blocking call that did not exist. Timing ten spawns from inside node gave 121ms. Do not trust a shell loop for sub-second benchmarks. DESIGN CALLS: the mark carries the state without colour (filled diamond in flight, hollow idle) so a terminal that drops colour still reads; counts render only when non-zero, because a line that always says '0 review · 0 backlog' is furniture and furniture stops being read; only the title is ever clipped, never the id or the counts; NO_COLOR is honoured. HARMLESS RULE, tested by spawning: a missing tracker, an unparseable tracker and a document with no projects each print NOTHING and exit 0 — a status line that throws leaves a broken terminal and no explanation. 133 tests pass, 10 new. WHY THIS ANGLE: the UserPromptSubmit hook was already an ambient surface and the highest-frequency one in the product; this is the same idea given a permanent place. NOT YET SEEN IN THE RUNTIME — like the hooks, it needs a session rooted at shipward_app to render for real.

cards.title: Hooks — make the Shipward protocol continuous, not aspirational

note.text: WHY, with evidence from this very session: CLAUDE.md, the MCP instructions field and the tool descriptions are three layers of ADVICE and nothing checks. Proof they are not enough — I built the entire MCP server for SW-005 without ever calling start; the card sat in Backlog while 500 lines were written against it, and I only noticed by running standup for an unrelated reason. If the author of the protocol, holding it in active context, drifts inside one session, advice is not a mechanism. FOUR HOOKS: SessionStart injects a standup so a session begins already knowing; UserPromptSubmit injects one line naming the active card EVERY TURN, which is the actual continuous part because drift cannot accumulate; PreToolUse on Edit/Write warns when source is about to change with no card in claude/working — WARNS, never blocks, because a hook that gets disabled protects nothing; Stop refuses to end while a card is still working with no done. DESIGN RULES: a hook must never be able to break a session, so every one exits 0 silently on any error; the Stop hook honours stop_hook_active so it cannot loop; and the standup text is extracted into a shared module so the hook and the MCP tool cannot drift apart. KNOWN LIMIT stated up front: hooks can make Claude TOUCH Shipward, they cannot make it write a good note — done with 'fixed it' satisfies every one of them and teaches the next session nothing.

SHIPPED. .claude/settings.json wires four hooks to .claude/hooks/shipward.mjs: SessionStart injects a standup unasked; UserPromptSubmit injects one line naming the active card EVERY turn (the continuous part — drift cannot accumulate); PreToolUse on Edit/Write/NotebookEdit warns when source changes with no card in claude/working; Stop refuses to end while a card is still working with no done. TWO RULES THE HOOK FILE MUST NEVER BREAK, both covered by tests: (1) a hook can never break a session — every path exits 0 and any failure (missing tracker, unparseable tracker, unknown subcommand) exits silently, because a broken hook that bricks the project is worse than no hook; (2) pre-edit WARNS and never denies — permissionDecision is always 'allow' — because a hook that gets in the way gets switched off and a switched-off hook protects nothing. Stop honours stop_hook_active or it would refuse the session forever. pre-edit exempts .shipward/, .claude/, _bmad-output/, .git/ and CLAUDE.md/README.md: touching those proves nothing about the protocol, so nagging is pure noise. REFACTOR THAT CAME WITH IT: standupText/line/stamp/PERISHABLE moved out of mcp.mjs into shipward/standup.mjs so the SessionStart hook and the MCP tool render from ONE implementation — two renderings of the same board would tell a session two different stories. 123 tests pass, 11 new, spawning the real script the way the runtime does (payload on stdin, JSON on stdout). MEASURED COST: ~90ms per prompt hook, dominated by node startup rather than reading the tracker; paid on every turn. NOT YET VERIFIED IN THE RUNTIME — the hooks are unit-tested against the documented wire shapes but have never actually fired inside Claude Code. That needs a session rooted at shipward_app plus hook approval. KNOWN LIMIT, stated up front: hooks can make Claude TOUCH Shipward, they cannot make it write a good note; done with 'fixed it' satisfies all four and teaches the next session nothing.

NOT YET PROVEN IN THE RUNTIME even though it is now on main: the hooks are unit-tested against the documented wire shapes but have never fired inside Claude Code. First session rooted at shipward_app will need to approve them.

cards.title: Close the memory loop — standup carries it, recall retrieves it

note.text: THE GAP, measured: the tracker holds 27 memory entries / 4044 words, and standup returns 0 of them. The only path back is start, one card at a time, so Claude retrieves memory about the ticket it is opening and never about the code it is about to touch. From the agent's side this store is write-only. FIX: (1) standup gains a bounded memory section — decisions not to reverse, and still-open items, each with its card id and date; (2) a new recall tool takes file / kind / query and returns the entries attached, ranked by what it would cost to miss. DESIGN RULES: every entry arrives with its date and card so a session can judge rather than believe; evidence is labelled as a claim about a PAST state, because 'tests pass' rots (45 was true this morning, it is 96 now); nothing is silently truncated — recall says what it dropped and how to get it. Standup stays readable: entries are clipped with the card id kept so the full text is one recall away.

SHIPPED. standup now carries a bounded memory section (still-open items + decisions not to reverse, each stamped with card and date, clipped so the full text is one recall away) and a new recall({file|kind|query}) tool retrieves the rest, ranked by what it would cost to miss, always reporting what it dropped. TWO THINGS THAT ONLY SHOWED UP ON REAL DATA: (1) BRIDGING FILE TO PROSE — SW-010's note, the most valuable in this repo, names NO file at all; it names isStale(), breakLock(), sweepTmp(), because that is how you write down what went wrong. recall({file}) therefore reads the file off disk and asks about every name declared inside it, not just the filename. Before the bridge, recall({file:'tracker-store'}) returned one irrelevant hit; after, six with both SW-010 findings ranked first. (2) DROPPING GENERIC NAMES — tracker-store.mjs declares 73 names and most are now()/read()/line(), so matching any of them returned the whole tracker and the top hits were unrelated. Tokens appearing across more than a quarter of the memory are now dropped before scoring, and entries rank by how many distinct names they match. GOTCHA IN THAT FIX: the share filter then ate EVERY token on a small corpus, because with two entries one hit is already 50 percent — recall returned nothing at all. Nothing counts as generic until it has turned up at least 4 times; regression test covers the young-repo case. Evidence entries are labelled 'as of then, not a claim about now' at the point of use, because '45 tests pass' was true this morning and is 112 now. Excerpts lead with the marker that classified them rather than the first 200 characters, which were usually provenance preamble. CLAUDE.md gains step 0: recall before editing an unfamiliar file. 112 tests pass, 16 new.

cards.title: Memory view — render what Claude knows, not just what is in flight

note.text: EXPLORATION, not a commitment: the memory-first angle from the 2026-07-27 divergence exercise. EVIDENCE THAT MOTIVATED IT, measured on the real tracker: notes are 22355 of 33836 file bytes = 66% of the tracker, and the UI renders them in a textarea inside a dialog behind a click, while a status field nobody rereads gets a whole column. The notes have also grown a grammar with nothing in the schema asking for one — SHIPPED x6, VERIFIED x5, REPRODUCED x3, DECIDED x2, TRADEOFF x2, plus ROOT CAUSE / GOTCHA / LESSON / NEEDS ALBERTO / SUPERSEDED / LEFT STALE and 17 other markers across 23 distinct kinds — and 33 distinct file paths already embedded in prose as untyped text. DESIGN: no schema change. A derived view parses the existing prose, classifies each ' || '-separated segment by marker lexicon, and groups by KIND rather than by card, because what a new session needs is 'every decision taken here' and 'what is still open', not 'SW-010's note'. Classification is a lens, shown as detected, never rewriting the note. Ships as a tab, NOT the default view, so it has to earn the home screen the way the Raw data view failed to.

BUILT as a tab, not the default. public/memory-lib.js parses the existing prose; no schema change. THE FINDING THAT MATTERED MOST was not the classifier but SUPERSESSION: openness is a property of the card's latest state, not of the segment that raised it. SW-008's note opens 'NEEDS ALBERTO' and two segments later says 'DECIDED' then 'SHIPPED' — counting that as open would send a fresh session to re-ask an answered question. An open item settled later on the same card is dimmed and labelled 'answered later on this card', not hidden, because 'this got resolved here' is itself worth reading. Took the open count 5 to 2. THREE HONEST LIMITS OF PARSING PROSE, all reproduced on real data: (1) MENTION VS USE — SW-013's own brief lists the marker vocabulary and so classified itself as open; a heuristic cannot tell naming a marker from using one. (2) CROSS-CARD RESOLUTION is invisible — SW-011's 'LEFT STALE: SPEC CAP-5' was closed by SW-012, and only within-card supersession is detectable. (3) THE SEPARATOR IS UNESCAPED — this very note's mention of the segment separator splits the note in half, visible in the UI as a sentence cut off at 'classifies each'. All three vanish if note becomes structured entries {t, kind, text, resolves} rather than prose with a delimiter; that is the real fork in the road and it is Alberto's call, not mine. 96 tests pass, 15 of them new. VERIFIED in the browser on real data: 26 entries across 5 groups, file filter 26->7 for lib.js, search 'mtime' -> 2 entries with SW-010 first, focus retained while typing, group headline and lede and tab all agreeing on 2.

cards.title: A live lock is broken as stale — silent lost write

note.text: REPRODUCED while fixing SW-009. The 12-writer store test fails about 1 run in 6 under full-suite load: 11 of 12 cards land, every child exits 0, nothing is logged. A high-cycle harness (6 processes x 150 mutations) loses ~1 write per 900 reliably. ROOT CAUSE: isStale() judges the lock from TWO separate observations of the path — readHolder() then lstat() — and the lock can be replaced between them. When readHolder() hits the lock in its momentary absence (normal, between one holder release and the next publish) it returns null, and lstat() then measures a DIFFERENT, brand-new lock. That new lock trips `if (age < 0) return true` — the line commented "clock skew: as broken as too old". Measured: st.mtimeMs carries sub-millisecond precision while Date.now() truncates to whole ms, so a freshly created lock reads as up to 0.62ms in the FUTURE in 1085 of 2000 observations. Over half of all new locks are therefore condemned the instant that race is hit. Trace confirms the full chain: break-won by a waiter, then 6ms later the true holder gets release-skip (its lock is gone) and its atomic-write chmod fails ENOENT because breakLock -> sweepTmp deleted the live holder’s in-flight .tmp. Two writers in the critical section, one write silently overwritten. THREE DEFECTS: (1) isStale reads stat and content from different observations; (2) age < 0 is treated as death when it actually means brand new; (3) sweepTmp unlinks temp and lock-scratch files belonging to LIVE processes.

FIXED. inspect() now reads mtime, inode and holder from ONE open handle, so a stat and a read can never land on two different locks. A future mtime means new, not dead (the old 'age < 0 = as broken as too old' line was the trigger). breakLock() compares the grave's inode against the snapshot it judged and puts an innocent lock back. sweepTmp() only collects files whose pid is dead. withLock() hands callers a held() guard checked immediately before the commit, so a lost lock raises LockLostError instead of overwriting whoever holds it now. EVIDENCE: before, ~1 write lost per 900 under sustained contention (2 of 4 trials) and the 12-writer test failed ~1 run in 6 under full-suite load; after, 12960 contended writes across 14 trials with zero lost and six consecutive clean suite runs. 49 tests pass. Three new regression tests were each run against the PREVIOUS store and all three fail there: future-dated lock read as a corpse, sweep eating a live process's in-flight temp, and a mid-write lock loss writing anyway.

SHIPPED stage B. shipward/mcp.mjs is newline-delimited JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdio, protocol 2025-11-25, zero deps, no SDK. Five tools mirror the five slash commands (standup/log/start/done/sync); each does the tracker half and leaves git plus the work itself to Claude. All rules — id allocation, branch naming, status transitions, feed copy — are imported from public/lib.js so the desk and Claude cannot drift; addMsg/editMsg/deleteMsg were moved into lib.js for that and app.js now calls them. .mcp.json registers it as the shipward server. DESIGN CALLS: an unknown tool name returns a readable errored RESULT rather than -32601, because it is the model mistake to correct not a protocol failure; an unknown card id lists what IS startable; start is idempotent so a re-run after a crash re-reports context instead of refusing; done APPENDS to the note rather than replacing it; sync applies every update and creation in ONE locked write with ONE feed entry. BUG FOUND BY SMOKE-TESTING THE REAL BINARY: stdin end called process.exit immediately and killed a call still in flight — losing a write that had taken the tracker lock and never answering. Every test held stdin open so none of them saw it; now the queue drains first, and the regression test was verified to fail against the old code. 24 MCP tests over a real pipe (split frames, two messages in one chunk, notifications, malformed input, batch refusal, stdout purity); 80 tests in total. This card was itself started and finished THROUGH the MCP server.

cards.title: Cross-process safe tracker writes — shared store + lock

note.text: Stage A of SW-005. Extracted read/validate/atomic-write into shipward/tracker-store.mjs behind an O_EXCL advisory lock spanning the whole read-modify-write; serve.mjs is now a client and its in-process promise chain is gone. That chain only protected same-process writes — the MCP server and Claude Code direct edits both sit outside it. Lock records pid+timestamp, aged out after 5s so a crashed holder cannot deadlock the desk. 34 tests pass: store.test.mjs spawns real child processes (12 concurrent writers all land, stale locks broken, fresh locks waited for not stolen, invalid mutations write nothing and still release); desk-core suite passes unchanged as the regression gate. ⚠️ PULLED BACK FROM REVIEW 2026-07-25: adversarial review REPRODUCED five failures — the lock does not hold. (1) Contended stale-break: 4 processes vs one stale lock, 9/25 trials LOST WRITES, because detect-and-break is three non-atomic steps and each breaker unlinks the previous winner’s fresh lock. (2) A 6s mutation gets its lock stolen at 5s; both processes exit 0 and one write vanishes silently. (3) A dangling symlink at the lock path spins acquire() forever at 100% CPU — two of three loop paths skip the deadline check. (4) replace() (every card drag) never re-reads under the lock, so a desk PUT erased a Claude write that had committed correctly. (5) rename resets file mode 600→644. Also: feed at exactly 200 makes validate() reject every subsequent write and freezes the tracker; lost in-process FIFO ordering; GET re-serializes instead of returning raw bytes. 34 tests passed throughout — none of them covered contention.

REWORKED after review: the lock was redesigned, not patched. Publish via write-scratch-then-link(): link is atomic AND never leaves an empty lock visible, which open(wx) did — under contention a process starved between create and stamp, waiters read a bodyless lock and broke a LIVE holder’s. Break a dead lock by rename (one atomic step) so two breakers cannot both win and delete each other’s fresh lock. Ownership token: a holder only ever releases the lock it took. Liveness (process.kill(pid,0)) over age, plus a utimes heartbeat — utimes not writeFile, because rewriting the body truncates it and reopens the same window. Every retry path now checks the deadline and sleeps (two used to spin at 100% CPU). Also: feed cap truncates instead of rejecting (rejection froze the tracker permanently at 200 entries); file mode preserved across rename; fsync before rename; read() distinguishes ENOENT from EACCES; GET returns raw bytes not a re-serialization; in-process FIFO queue restored in front of the lock; err.name instead of instanceof; orphan tmp and lock-scratch files swept on break. 41 tests pass. Stress: 25 trials x 4 contended writers against a stale lock = 0 lost writes, 0 leftovers (was 9/25 losing writes). 12-writer repro 12/12 across three runs.

cards.title: Prefer MCP in CLAUDE.md and make the header tag live

note.text: Stage C of SW-005, depends on SW-005 stage B. Rewrite CLAUDE.md so the protocol prefers the MCP tools with direct file edits as the documented fallback (Alberto authorised this Ask First change at the SW-005 step-01 checkpoint). Drive the header MCP CONNECTED tag from an mcp.lastSeen heartbeat, stale after 150s, with a muted non-blinking disconnected variant. schema.json sets no additionalProperties, so the mcp key needs no schema change — verified. KNOWN TRADEOFF: a 60s heartbeat makes the committed tracker.json dirty in git about once a minute; the alternative is a .shipward/mcp-status.json sidecar.

SHIPPED stage C. CLAUDE.md now leads with the five MCP tools and keeps direct file edits as the documented fallback for when no server is connected, with the rules stated once so they apply to both routes. The MCP CONNECTED tag was HARDCODED — lit whether or not anything was listening, which made it decoration on a product whose premise is that Claude really is on the other end. It now reads doc.mcp.lastSeen via mcpStatus() in lib.js, stamped by the MCP server every 60s, dark after 150s (MCP_STALE_MS). Offline is muted with no animation: a blinking light that means nothing trains you to ignore the one that means something. A future-dated heartbeat reads as live rather than infinitely stale — a disagreeing clock is not a dead server. TRADEOFF TAKEN AS DECIDED: the heartbeat lives in tracker.json, so a committed tracker goes dirty in git about once a minute during a session; the .shipward/mcp-status.json sidecar alternative was rejected because one occasionally dirty file beats two files that can disagree. The heartbeat is best-effort and never fails a session. VERIFIED end to end: with no mcp key the tag read MCP OFFLINE, muted, animation none; starting a real mcp.mjs against that tracker flipped it to MCP CONNECTED, accent colour, swm-blink, title 'last seen just now', within one 3s poll. Test note: the server writes on startup, so the read-only assertions now compare board state with the mcp key stripped rather than raw bytes. 84 tests pass.

cards.title: PUT /api/tracker is last-write-wins — decide if it should be

note.text: REPRODUCED by adversarial review against a live server: desk GETs at T0, Claude Code appends a card via mutate() at T1 (correctly locked, committed), desk PUTs its T0 snapshot at T2 — PUT 200 and Claude’s card is GONE. The lock worked perfectly and the data was still destroyed, because replace() never re-reads under the lock: its base document came from an unlocked GET seconds earlier. This is the primary remaining loss path. It is also a CONTRADICTION between two live contracts. spec-mcp-tracker-server.md Always says two processes must never start a mutation from the same base document; spec-shipward-desk-core.md accepts no optimistic concurrency on PUT, last write wins, as a documented assumption. NEEDS ALBERTO: either add optimistic concurrency (If-Match on a version or etag, 409 on conflict, UI re-reads and retries) which is an Ask First change to the HTTP surface, or narrow the stage-A Always to say the lock protects mutate() callers only and PUT stays last-write-wins by design. Referenced from a comment in tracker-store.mjs replace().

DECIDED by Alberto: add optimistic concurrency. GET returns an ETag (content hash); PUT requires If-Match and answers 409 with the current document when it does not match; the UI re-applies its mutation to the fresh document and retries once. This is the authorised Ask First change to the HTTP surface. [committed by Claude at T1]

SHIPPED: GET returns an ETag (sha256 of the file bytes, 16 hex chars, quoted). PUT requires If-Match — 428 without it — and the store compares it INSIDE the lock against what is on disk. Mismatch answers 409 carrying the document that actually won plus its ETag, so the client can re-apply rather than guess. The UI recovers automatically: commit() takes a mutation, not a snapshot, so on 409 it re-applies the same intent to the winning document and retries once; a second conflict adopts the winner and says so. VERIFIED end to end against the live server by replaying the exact scenario the review used to destroy data: desk GETs at T0, Claude commits via mutate() at T1, desk PUTs its T0 snapshot at T2 — now HTTP 409 and Claude’s write SURVIVES. In the browser: drag sends a well-formed If-Match; a forced stale etag produced 409 then 200 with the external write intact and no error shown. 45 tests pass. The old "concurrent writes never corrupt the file" test was rewritten — it asserted six concurrent PUTs from one base all succeed, which was the bug; it now asserts exactly one wins and the rest get 409.
Commit backfilled during the merge sync — the card had carried a null sha since it was closed.

cards.title: serve.test.mjs binds a fixed port and cannot run concurrently

note.text: The sandbox server in serve.test.mjs hard-codes port 4749. A leftover server from an earlier or parallel run holds the port, the new server fails to bind, and the tests silently assert against the STALE server — observed here as three phantom failures (GET returning 200 for a missing tracker). Fix: bind port 0, read the assigned port back from the server, pass it to the tests. The sandbox server should also log bind failures rather than dying silently.

SHIPPED: serve.mjs now reads SHIPWARD_PORT (default 4747) and logs the port it actually bound; the test spawns it with SHIPWARD_PORT=0 and parses the port back out of stdout, so the suite no longer rewrites serve.mjs source to patch the constant. A bind failure logs to stderr and exits 1 — covered by a test that starts a second server on the taken port and asserts exit 1 plus 'already in use'. 46 tests pass. FOUND WHILE DOING THIS: the 12-writer store test failed intermittently (~1 run in 6 under full-suite load, 11/12 cards). Not flaky — a real silent lost write. Root cause traced and filed as SW-010.
